description: Working on the problem identifying and navigate the location on the Lunar surface, the problem is not only the best place to be at in terms of resources, but also be able to setup a variety of research stations and have constant contact
summary: LODESTAR (Lunar Outpost Decision Engine for Site Targeting And Reachability) is an interactive 3D web tool that helps mission planners find where on the Moon to build an outpost. It combines real NASA data, including LRO LOLA elevation, LROC imagery and twelve Lunar Prospector element and water maps, in a five-step wizard. Users first weight the resources they care about, such as water ice, ilmenite or thorium. Next they set terrain limits for elevation and slope, then a minimum Earth-communication availability through the Deep Space Network or a lunar relay. LODESTAR then highlights connected areas on a rotating globe that pass every constraint, so there is room for multiple research stations rather than a single landing point. For a chosen site, it estimates delta-V, transfer time and the mass a launcher must deliver to trans-lunar injection. It compares 16 launch vehicles across four orbital configurations, giving a clear verdict on which rockets can get there. As Artemis moves toward a sustained human presence, site choice must balance resources, safety, continuous contact with Earth and launch cost together. LODESTAR makes those trade-offs visible in one place.
details:
LODESTAR (Lunar Outpost Decision Engine for Site Targeting And Reachability) is a browser-based 3D tool that helps users choose where on the Moon to put an outpost. It brings science, terrain, communications and launch logistics together in one guided workflow. Users work on an interactive globe through five steps, and each step narrows the set of suitable sites.

In Resources, users weight twelve Lunar Prospector maps and set minimum and maximum limits for each. The maps cover hydrogen and epithermal neutrons as water indicators, plus iron, titanium, thorium, potassium, magnesium, aluminium, calcium, silicon, uranium and samarium. Presets for water ice, ilmenite and thorium give a quick start. In Terrain, users set limits on elevation and slope using LRO LOLA data, with an LROC colour basemap. In Communications, users set a minimum link availability, either direct-to-Earth through the Deep Space Network (34 m or 70 m antennas, S, X or Ka band) or through a lunar relay orbit. Approximate contact times are shown for any pinned point. In Site Selection, LODESTAR finds connected areas that pass every limit, not single points, so there is room for multiple research stations. Clicking an area shows its region, Earth-communication summary and delta-V. In Mission, users enter a landed mass and choose among four orbital configurations, shown on an Earth–Moon diagram. LODESTAR then computes delta-V, transfer time and the mass required at trans-lunar injection, and checks the result against 16 launch vehicles drawn to scale.

We checked the results against known lunar science. The water preset picks out the polar regions near 85.7°S and 86.7°N. Ilmenite highlights Oceanus Procellarum and Mare Tranquillitatis, and thorium highlights the Procellarum–Imbrium region. Requiring 90% direct-to-Earth availability excludes the entire far side, as expected.

The main benefit is speed and transparency in early trade studies. Questions that normally need several separate datasets and tools can be explored in minutes. Because every constraint is visible, users can see exactly why a site passes or fails. The intended impact is to support early planning for a sustained presence under Artemis, where resource use, safety, continuous contact with Earth and launch cost all have to be balanced together. It is also meant to help students and the public understand why some sites are favoured over others.

LODESTAR is a static website built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules), with three.js for the 3D globe. It needs no build step and no installation, and it is hosted on GitHub Pages. Python scripts download real NASA data (LRO LOLA, LROC and Lunar Prospector) and convert it into web-ready grids. Launch-vehicle data is stored in JSON, with a source link for each vehicle and each figure marked as published or estimated. We tested all five steps in headless Chromium against the real data.

The creative step is chaining science data, surface engineering, communications and launch logistics into one continuous decision, so a resource map ends in an answer to “which rocket can get us there?”. Treating communications as a first-class constraint, and returning areas rather than points, both reflect what an actual outpost needs.

We considered the tool’s limits and state them openly. The resource maps have 15–150 km pixels, so results are regional guidance, not landing-site certification. The Moon is modelled as a sphere without terrain horizons, relay links are real-time only, DSN contact time is a geometric upper bound, and some launcher and orbit figures are labelled estimates. Future development will include data from JAXA, ISRO (Chandrayaan-2 and 3) for more finer resolution and detailed analysis reporting.
